{{Short description|Accumulation of harmful mutations}}
[[File:Morgan crossover 1.jpg|thumb|Illustration of chromosome crossover during genetic recombination]]

In [[evolution]]ary [[genetics]], '''Muller's ratchet''' (named after American geneticist [[Hermann Joseph Muller]], by analogy with a [[ratchet effect]]) is a process which, in the absence of [[Genetic recombination|recombination]] (especially in an [[Asexual reproduction|asexual]] [[Population (biology)|population]]), results in an accumulation of irreversible [[Mutation#By effect on fitness (harmful, beneficial, neutral mutations)|deleterious mutations]].<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Muller HJ |year=1932 |title=Some genetic aspects of sex |journal=[[American Naturalist]] |volume=66 |issue=703 |pages=118–138 |doi=10.1086/280418|bibcode=1932ANat...66..118M |s2cid=84301227 }} (Muller's original 1932 paper)</ref><ref name="Muller_1964">{{cite journal | vauthors = Muller HJ | title = The relation of recombination to mutational advance | journal = Mutation Research | volume = 106 | pages = 2–9 | date = May 1964 | issue = 1 | pmid = 14195748 | doi = 10.1016/0027-5107(64)90047-8 | bibcode = 1964MRFMM...1....2M }} (original paper as cited by, e.g.: {{cite book | vauthors = Smith JM, Szathmary E |year=1997 | title=The major transitions in evolution |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford, New York, Tokyo}}; {{cite book| vauthors = Futuyma DJ|year=1998 |title=Evolutionary biology|edition=3rd |publisher=Sinauer Associates|location=Sunderland, Mass.}})</ref> That happens because in the absence of recombination, and assuming reverse mutations are rare, offspring bear at least as much [[mutational load]] as their parents.<ref name="Muller_1964" />

Muller proposed the mechanism as one reason why [[sexual reproduction]] may be [[evolution of sex|favored]] over [[asexual reproduction]], as sexual organisms benefit from recombination and consequent elimination of deleterious mutations. The negative effect of accumulating irreversible deleterious mutations may not be prevalent in organisms which, while they reproduce asexually, also undergo other forms of recombination. This effect has also been observed in those regions of the genomes of sexual organisms that do not undergo recombination.

==Etymology==
Although Muller discussed the advantages of sexual reproduction in his 1932 talk, it does not contain the word "ratchet". Muller first introduced the term "ratchet" in his 1964 paper,<ref name="Muller_1964" /> and the phrase "Muller's ratchet" was coined by [[Joe Felsenstein]] in his 1974 paper, "The Evolutionary Advantage of Recombination".<ref name="pmid4448362">{{cite journal | vauthors = Felsenstein J | title = The evolutionary advantage of recombination | journal = Genetics | volume = 78 | issue = 2 | pages = 737–56 | date = October 1974 | doi = 10.1093/genetics/78.2.737 | pmid = 4448362 | pmc = 1213231 }}</ref>

==Explanation==
Asexual reproduction compels genomes to be inherited as indivisible blocks so that once the least mutated genomes in an asexual population begin to carry at least one deleterious mutation, no genomes with fewer such mutations can be expected to be found in future generations (except as a result of [[Mutation#By effect on function|back mutation]]). This results in an eventual accumulation of mutations known as [[genetic load]]. In theory, the genetic load carried by asexual populations eventually becomes so great that the population goes extinct.<ref name=analysis>{{Cite book|last1 = Freeman|first1 = Scott|first2 = Jon C | last2 = Herron | name-list-style = vanc |title = Evolutionary Analysis, 4th edition|location = San Francisco|publisher = Benjamin Cummings| year= 2007| pages = 308–309| isbn = 978-0-13-227584-2 }}</ref> Also, laboratory experiments have confirmed the existence of the ratchet and the consequent extinction of populations in many organisms (under intense drift and when recombinations are not allowed) including [[RNA viruses]], [[bacteria]], and [[eukaryotes]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chao L | title = Fitness of RNA virus decreased by Muller's ratchet | journal = Nature | volume = 348 | issue = 6300 | pages = 454–5 | date = November 1990 | pmid = 2247152 | doi = 10.1038/348454a0 | bibcode = 1990Natur.348..454C | s2cid = 4235839 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Andersson DI, Hughes D | title = Muller's ratchet decreases fitness of a DNA-based microbe | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 93 | issue = 2 | pages = 906–7 | date = January 1996 | pmid = 8570657 | pmc = 40156 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.93.2.906 | bibcode = 1996PNAS...93..906A | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zeyl C, Mizesko M, de Visser JA | title = Mutational meltdown in laboratory yeast populations | journal = Evolution; International Journal of Organic Evolution | volume = 55 | issue = 5 | pages = 909–17 | date = May 2001 | pmid = 11430651 | doi = 10.1554/0014-3820(2001)055[0909:MMILYP]2.0.CO;2 | s2cid = 198152956 }}</ref> In sexual populations, the process of genetic recombination allows the genomes of the [[offspring]] to be different from the genomes of the parents. In particular, progeny (offspring) genomes with fewer mutations can be generated from more highly mutated parental genomes by putting together mutation-free portions of parental chromosomes. Also, [[Negative selection (natural selection)|purifying selection]], to some extent, unburdens a loaded population when recombination results in different combinations of mutations.<ref name="Muller_1964" />

Among [[protists]] and [[prokaryotes]], a plethora of supposedly asexual organisms exists. More and more are being shown to exchange genetic information through a variety of mechanisms. In contrast, the genomes of [[Mitochondrion|mitochondria]] and [[chloroplast]]s do not recombine and would undergo Muller's ratchet were they not as small as they are (see Birdsell and Wills [pp.&nbsp;93–95]).<ref>Birdsell JA, Wills C (2003). The evolutionary origin and maintenance of sexual recombination: A review of contemporary models.  Evolutionary Biology Series >> Evolutionary Biology, Vol. 33 pp. 27-137.  MacIntyre, Ross J.; Clegg, Michael, T (Eds.), Springer. Hardcover {{ISBN|978-0306472619}}, {{ISBN|0306472619}}  Softcover {{ISBN|978-1-4419-3385-0}}.</ref> Indeed, the probability that the least mutated genomes in an asexual population end up carrying at least one (additional) mutation depends heavily on the genomic mutation rate and this increases more or less linearly with the size of the genome (more accurately, with the number of base pairs present in active genes). However, reductions in genome size, especially in parasites and symbionts, can also be caused by direct selection to get rid of genes that have become unnecessary. Therefore, a smaller genome is not a sure indication of the action of Muller's ratchet.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Moran NA | title = Accelerated evolution and Muller's rachet in endosymbiotic bacteria | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 93 | issue = 7 | pages = 2873–8 | date = April 1996 | pmid = 8610134 | pmc = 39726 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.93.7.2873 | bibcode = 1996PNAS...93.2873M | doi-access = free }} (An article that discusses Muller's ratchet in the context of endosymbiotic bacteria.)</ref>

In sexually reproducing organisms, nonrecombining chromosomes or chromosomal regions such as the mammalian [[Y chromosome]] (with the exception of multicopy sequences which do engage intrachromosomal recombination and gene conversion<ref name=analysis/>) should also be subject to the effects of Muller's ratchet. Such nonrecombining sequences tend to shrink and evolve quickly. However, this fast evolution might also be due to these sequences' inability to repair DNA damage via template-assisted repair, which is equivalent to an increase in the mutation rate for these sequences. Ascribing cases of genome shrinkage or fast evolution to Muller's ratchet alone is not easy.

Muller's ratchet relies on [[genetic drift]], and turns faster in smaller populations because in such populations deleterious mutations have a better chance of fixation. Therefore, it sets the limits to the maximum size of asexual genomes and to the long-term evolutionary continuity of asexual lineages.<ref name=analysis /> However, some asexual lineages are thought to be quite ancient; [[Bdelloidea|Bdelloid]] rotifers, for example, appear to have been asexual for nearly 40 million years.<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Milius S |title= Bdelloids: No sex for over 40 million years. |url= http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Bdelloids%3A+No+sex+for+over+40+million+years.-a062685144 |work=TheFreeLibrary |publisher=ScienceNews |access-date=30 April 2011 }}</ref> However, rotifers were found to possess a substantial number of foreign genes from possible [[horizontal gene transfer]] events.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Boschetti C, Carr A, Crisp A, Eyres I, Wang-Koh Y, Lubzens E, Barraclough TG, Micklem G, Tunnacliffe A | display-authors = 6 | title = Biochemical diversification through foreign gene expression in bdelloid rotifers | journal = PLOS Genetics | volume = 8 | issue = 11 | article-number = e1003035 | date = November 15, 2012 | pmid = 23166508 | pmc = 3499245 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pgen.1003035 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Furthermore, a vertebrate fish, ''[[Poecilia formosa]]'', seems to defy the ratchet effect, having existed for 500,000 generations. This has been explained by maintenance of genomic diversity through parental [[introgression]] and a high level of heterozygosity resulting from the hybrid origin of this species.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Warren WC, García-Pérez R, Xu S, Lampert KP, Chalopin D, Stöck M, Loewe L, Lu Y, Kuderna L, Minx P, Montague MJ, Tomlinson C, Hillier LW, Murphy DN, Wang J, Wang Z, Garcia CM, Thomas GC, Volff JN, Farias F, Aken B, Walter RB, Pruitt KD, Marques-Bonet T, Hahn MW, Kneitz S, Lynch M, Schartl M | display-authors = 6 | title = Clonal polymorphism and high heterozygosity in the celibate genome of the Amazon molly | journal = Nature Ecology & Evolution | volume = 2 | issue = 4 | pages = 669–679 | date = April 2018 | pmid = 29434351 | doi = 10.1038/s41559-018-0473-y | doi-access = free | pmc = 5866774 | bibcode = 2018NatEE...2..669W }}</ref>

==Calculation of the fittest class==
In 1978, John Haigh used a [[Genetic drift#Wright.E2.80.93Fisher model|Wright–Fisher model]] to analyze the effect of Muller's ratchet in an asexual population.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | vauthors = Haigh J | title = The accumulation of deleterious genes in a population--Muller's Ratchet | journal = Theoretical Population Biology | volume = 14 | issue = 2 | pages = 251–67 | date = October 1978 | pmid = 746491 | doi = 10.1016/0040-5809(78)90027-8 | bibcode = 1978TPBio..14..251H }}</ref> If the ratchet is operating the fittest class (least loaded individuals) is small and prone to extinction by the effect of genetic drift. In his paper Haigh derives the equation that calculates the frequency of individuals carrying <math>k
</math> mutations for the population with stationary distribution:

<math>n_k\ =\ \frac{Ne^{-\theta}\theta^k}{k!} 
</math>

<math>\theta=\ \lambda / s
</math>

where, <math>n_k\ 
</math> is the number of individual carrying <math>k
</math> mutations, <math>N
</math> is the population size, <math>\lambda
</math> is the mutation rate and <math>(1-s)^k
</math> is the selection coefficient for a genome with <math>k
</math> mutations.
Thus, the frequency of the individuals of the fittest class (<math>k =0
</math>) is:

<math>{n_0}\ = N \ \ e^{-\ \theta} 
</math>

In an asexual population which suffers from ratchet the frequency of fittest individuals would be small, and go extinct after few generations.<ref name=":1" /> This is called a click of the ratchet. Following each click, the rate of accumulation of deleterious mutation would increase, and ultimately results in the extinction of the population.

==The antiquity of recombination and Muller's ratchet==
It has been argued that [[homologous recombination|recombination]] was an evolutionary development as ancient as [[life]] on Earth.<ref name="pmid12911039">{{cite journal | vauthors = Lehman N | title = A case for the extreme antiquity of recombination | journal = Journal of Molecular Evolution | volume = 56 | issue = 6 | pages = 770–7 | date = June 2003 | pmid = 12911039 | doi = 10.1007/s00239-003-2454-1 | bibcode = 2003JMolE..56..770L | s2cid = 33130898 }}</ref>  Early [[RNA world|RNA replicators]] capable of recombination may have been the ancestral sexual source  from which [[asexual reproduction|asexual]] lineages could periodically emerge.<ref name="pmid12911039" />  Recombination in the early sexual lineages may have provided a means for coping with genome damage.<ref name="pmid6209512">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bernstein H, Byerly HC, Hopf FA, Michod RE | title = Origin of sex | journal = Journal of Theoretical Biology | volume = 110 | issue = 3 | pages = 323–51 | date = October 1984 | pmid = 6209512 | doi = 10.1016/s0022-5193(84)80178-2 | bibcode = 1984JThBi.110..323B }}</ref>  Muller's ratchet under such ancient conditions would likely have impeded the evolutionary persistence of the asexual lineages that were unable to undergo recombination.<ref name="pmid12911039" />

==Muller's ratchet and mutational meltdown==
Since deleterious mutations are harmful by definition, accumulation of them would result in loss of individuals and a smaller population size. Small populations are more susceptible to the ratchet effect and more deleterious mutations would be fixed as a result of genetic drift. This creates a positive feedback loop which accelerates extinction of small asexual populations. This phenomenon has been called [[mutational meltdown]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gabriel W, Lynch M, Bürger R | title = Muller's Ratchet and Mutational Meltdowns | journal = Evolution; International Journal of Organic Evolution | volume = 47 | issue = 6 | pages = 1744–1757 | date = December 1993 | pmid = 28567994 | doi = 10.1111/j.1558-5646.1993.tb01266.x | bibcode = 1993Evolu..47.1744G | s2cid = 1323281 | url = https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/5135/1/Gabriel_wilfried_5135.pdf | doi-access = free }}</ref>  It appears that mutational meltdown due to Muller's ratchet can be avoided by a little bit of sex as in the common [[apomixis|apomictic]] asexual flowering plant ''[[Ranunculus auricomus]]''.<ref name = Hojsgaard2015>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hojsgaard D, Hörandl E |title=A little bit of sex matters for genome evolution in asexual plants |journal=Front Plant Sci |volume=6 |issue= |page=82 |date=2015 |pmid=25750646 |pmc=4335465 |doi=10.3389/fpls.2015.00082 |bibcode=2015FrPS....6...82H |doi-access=free |url=}}</ref>
